_comment: Claude Code registration of the shared, provider-neutral Python hooks (.claude/hooks/*.py speak every provider payload via _compat.py). The Codex counterpart (.codex/hooks.json + config.toml) is GENERATED from this file by team-kits/gen_provider_artifacts.py - never hand-maintained. Every interpreter runs with -B: .claude/hooks and .claude/kernel are the hashed enforcement bundle, and a hook that leaves a .pyc behind changes the bundle it was just trusted against - which is why bytecode used to be excluded from the hash instead (kernel/hashing.py BYTECODE_SUFFIXES). Measured cost of -B on a full kernel import: ~5 ms. The `model` key is the project's DEFAULT model, and it names the same tier the bound `agent` carries so the kit does not ship two answers to the question which model this session runs on. Measured 2026-08-21 (docs/reviews/2026-08-21-tsk0078-measurements.md): the bound agent's own `model:` frontmatter WINS over this key, and an explicit user model choice wins over both -- so this value governs only what names no model of its own. Every shipped role does (tools/validate.py refuses a specialist or a lead without `model:`), which leaves the Codex lead fallback in gen_provider_artifacts and any built-in agent. `tools/test_model_ladder.py::test_every_kit_settings_names_the_tier_its_bound_lead_pins_bug_0306` holds the sameness.

PreToolUse._comment: EVERY ENTRY NAMES A WINDOW, and that is one half of a construction rather than a rule of its own. A `timeout` is the moment the provider KILLS this hook, and a killed hook is read as "hook error, carry on" -- an ALLOW. Measured 2026-08-23 on claude.exe 2.1.239 (tools/provider_observations.json -> hook_deadlines): an entry with `timeout: 5` whose hook needed 20 s was KILLED and the refused command RAN, with nothing on the user's channel to say a gate had been killed; an entry naming NO timeout survived 310 s and 560 s and was killed at 900 s, so the provider's own default window exists too and sits near 600 s. Until 2026-09-12 that measurement was answered by leaving the window OFF nearly everywhere -- 2 of 89 entries across the three kits carried one -- and by every hook promising to stay far inside a window nothing noticed arriving (BUG-0153/H61). `_compat.start_the_deadline` now refuses BEFORE the window closes instead of racing it, and it refuses a registration that names no window at all: a gate that cannot know when it is killed cannot promise to answer first. The two halves ship together because either alone is worse than neither -- the reader without the windows shuts every hook of this kit, the windows without the reader are a kill moment per entry. The VALUE is derived and not chosen: `tools/test_hooks.py::test_every_registration_names_a_window_its_gate_can_answer_inside` requires every window to clear the chain's own child bounds plus the budget one hook process gives itself (`_compat.HOOK_DEADLINE_SECONDS`), which is what makes the gate's own refusal arrive before the kill. The ledger pair is ONE chained command and its ORDER IS load-bearing, unlike the filing chain's below: `_gate.py` stops at the first refusal, and a ledger whose rows are broken data has to be reported as that before anybody is sent back to a document to read it a second time (FR-0065). `gate_second_booking` acts on the SHELL moments of `gate_ledger_valid.requires_a_sound_ledger` only and deliberately not on a dispatch -- the second reading is written by a second spawn, so refusing the spawn would refuse the way out of the refusal; that is why it is not in the `Agent|Task` chain below. The only child it starts is a `git` read capped at `_bookings.GIT_TIMEOUT`, which the window rule above does NOT see -- it reads each GATE file's own `timeout=` keywords and this one's bound lives in `_bookings`; what covers it instead is the reader in `_compat`, which bounds the process rather than the child.

ONE chained command, and gate_dispatch is LAST because it is the only one here that SPENDS something (the task's dispatch lease). Measured 2026-08-02: every PreToolUse hook of an event runs to completion even when a sibling exits 2, so registered separately this gate paid for spawns the gates beside it were refusing in the same 52 ms. _gate.py runs the chain in one process and stops at the first refusal. A chain is also why a `timeout` here would be the worst of the file: one deadline for four gates, and a kill on it lets the spawn through unjudged -- see the Bash|PowerShell entry above for the measurement that took it out.

ONE chained command, and unlike the Agent|Task entry above the ORDER here is NOT load-bearing -- said plainly because the first version of this comment claimed it was and a swap of the two names in a clone left every test green (measured 2026-08-29). `gate_second_reading` stands down on its own for every case `gate_filing` refuses: an empty plan and a destination no rule covers both end in its own early return, not in the launcher stopping the chain (`test_the_second_reading_gate_stands_down_where_it_is_not_the_question`). What the chain DOES buy is one process instead of two, measured at +66..74 ms for the second gate against ~126 ms for a second launcher. `NotebookEdit` is on the matcher because `_compat.file_paths` reads `notebook_path` and a notebook lands a file like any other write -- measured rc 0 into a plan-covered path while it was missing. No `timeout` here for the reason the Bash|PowerShell entry states: a window is a kill window, a killed gate is a silent allow, and neither of these two waits on a child.

PostToolUse._comment: The recorders that make the four-eyes rules decidable: they stamp WHICH RUN wrote each staged reading, from the `agent_id` this call's payload carries -- `record_filing_reading` for a document's classification (FR-0035), `record_booking_reading` for a ledger row's figures (FR-0065). ONE chained command whose order is NOT load-bearing: both exit 0 unconditionally, so neither can stop the other, and they write into two different stores. Registered on every event a file can arrive through, and in its OWN entry rather than chained behind `gate_ledger_valid`, because a chain stops at the first non-zero exit and that gate exits 2 here on a broken ledger -- which has nothing to do with filing and would silently stop attesting.

This entry carried `timeout: 120` and no longer does -- see the Bash|PowerShell entry above for the measurement. What a kill costs HERE is a different thing and is worth stating: PostToolUse cannot deny, so this is the early warning that the ledger was just broken, and a killed one loses that warning rather than a refusal. It is dropped for the same reason all the same: nothing in this hook can notice it is about to be killed, so the only bound it keeps is its own (`gate_ledger_valid.TOTAL_BUDGET`).

SubagentStop._comment: ONE chained command, and gate_dispatch is LAST because the gate ahead of it can turn this stop into a CONTINUATION: gate_subagent_output exits 2 for a final message without its output contract, and the child then keeps working. gate_dispatch records the child's END here (BUG-0058), and a record written ahead of that refusal would report a specialist that is still running as idle at the lead's next turn-end. _gate.py runs the chain in one process and stops at the first refusal, which is exactly what makes the order carry the meaning.

Stop._comment: The way back for a dispatch lease that was spent on a spawn nobody ever started. `PermissionDenied` used to carry that job and was removed here: measured 2026-08-02, it fired in NONE of twelve real headless sessions, on either a hook refusal or a permission refusal, while PostToolUseFailure from this same file did fire. Stop fired in all twelve, including after four refused tool calls. gate_dispatch DOES exit 2 here, for one thing and no other: a dispatch whose own records say no child is on it, which the lead was about to leave unmentioned for another turn (BUG-0058). A Stop that exits 2 does not end the turn, which is the right answer to that and the wrong one to a rollback - so the reconciliation beside it stays silent. It refuses at most once per finding and never on a stop the provider marks as one a hook already blocked - see handle_stop and _name_the_dispatches_the_records_say_nobody_is_on.
